title: Thought and speech: Leah and Rachel, and the breath of the heart

lectures.id: Walters 5784 Edited/Ch 37/037.1 Shaar HaYichud ch 37.1 enhanced.mp3
Walters 5784 Edited/Ch 37/037.2 Shaar HaYichud ch 37.2 enhanced.mp3

overview: Chapter 37 takes up the union of Yisrael and Yaakov with Leah and Rachel, promised ten chapters earlier. Leah is thought and Rachel is speech, two levels of *Malchus*, which the *Zohar* finds in the two *heis*es of the Name and in the two women of Shir HaShirim. The chapter then turns to the voice. Yaakov's voice has an inner part that no one hears, the conscience G-d placed in us at Matan Torah, and an outer part that is spoken. The breath of the heart is made of fire, water and wind, the middos of chesed, gevura and tiferes: expansion when we are happy, contraction when we are sad, and a balance between them. Life runs on this breathing in and out. A feeling that stays in the heart is not yet a decree; once it is spoken, it is done. The way we read events shapes what we feel. The second class turns to the inner world: Leah as thought that cannot hold the middos, the four kinds of *yichud*, and the hidden side of creation and of Torah. It ends with Shabbos, the day that inner world is lived fully.

blocks.text: Yaakov has two names, and the chapter opens the topic it promised about ten chapters back: how Yisrael and Yaakov unite with Leah and Rachel. Each of these is a *partzuf*, a face made of all ten *sefiros* working together with a focus on one part of them. The *partzuf* focused on understanding is *Ima*, the one focused on *chachma* is *Abba*, and the middos are *Zeir Anpin*. Within *Zeir Anpin* the middos appear in two configurations, Yaakov and Yisrael: Yaakov is the middos as they are on their own, and Yisrael is the middos as they are with the *mochin*. Leah and Rachel correspond to thought and speech, two *partzufim* of *Malchus*.

audio.lecture: Walters 5784 Edited/Ch 37/037.1 Shaar HaYichud ch 37.1 enhanced.mp3

blocks.text: Leah is thought and Rachel is speech. Thought is connected more to *bina*, understanding, while speech is the expression of the middos. Both belong to *Malchus*.

audio.lecture: Walters 5784 Edited/Ch 37/037.1 Shaar HaYichud ch 37.1 enhanced.mp3

blocks.text: The first *hei* and the second *hei* of the Name are the two women. The Zohar says that Shlomo HaMelech, in Shir HaShirim, is speaking of two levels, or two women, so to speak. One is *bina* and *Malchus*; the other is *machshava* and *dibur*. That is why he describes his beloved differently in the two sections. The *kallah* that he brings from Lebanon is also *Malchus*, but the Zohar explains that this really connects to *Zeir Anpin*.

audio.lecture: Walters 5784 Edited/Ch 37/037.1 Shaar HaYichud ch 37.1 enhanced.mp3

blocks.text: The first *hei* is the older sister, Leah, and the last *hei* is the younger, Rachel: he paraphrases the verse on the two daughters and hangs the two *partzufim* on it. This is the general idea of the chapter: thought and speech.

audio.lecture: Walters 5784 Edited/Ch 37/037.1 Shaar HaYichud ch 37.1 enhanced.mp3

blocks.title: The thought you keep and the speech you share
blocks.text: Our thought is inside us, and other people do not hear it. It is tied to direct experience and feeling, much of which cannot be expressed: you can think of a color, but you cannot explain a color to someone who has never seen it. Speech is what we can reveal to someone else, but what passes over is only the external part, bound to the symbols of language. This goes back to the inner desire and the world of *Adam Kadmon* from chapters 17 to 19. The inner wish to feel at home becomes a wish for a house, and associating the inner with something outside is how a person builds a world view. Creating thoughts works the same way: we take external sounds or writing and use them to convey what is inside, and in doing so we attach our inner understanding to outside things.

audio.lecture: Walters 5784 Edited/Ch 37/037.1 Shaar HaYichud ch 37.1 enhanced.mp3

blocks.text: Recap that opens the second class. Yaakov and Yisrael are *partzufim* that correspond to the middos. Yaakov is the natural middos, less mature but with a higher source. Yisrael is the middos with the *mochin*: when a person gains maturity and understanding, he can become more refined and change his nature. The class has been on how this is expressed in Rachel and Leah, thought and speech, and in the power of speech, which is heard in the voice and decides whether a person feels like speaking.

blocks.text: Yaakov's voice has two parts. The inner voice is not heard by anyone else. It is the self-talk in which a person interprets things, a big subject in psychology, and that interpretation is what gives rise to how he feels about them. The outer voice is what he expresses to other people. The Zohar teaches that the voice of *binah*, of *Imma*, is the inner one that is not heard.

audio.lecture: Walters 5784 Edited/Ch 37/037.1 Shaar HaYichud ch 37.1 enhanced.mp3

blocks.text: At Matan Torah there was a great voice, the sound of the shofar, which never ended. The Zohar says this great voice is the inner voice that is not heard. The main voice of Matan Torah was not speech that the ear takes in. G-d put into each of us a conscience, a sense of what is G-dly, good and right, that compels us to grow and seek the truth because it is true. That is the voice that says *v'lo yasaf*, and it has not stopped: tune in and you hear G-d speaking through your *neshama*. Our emotions can process it into an outer voice that we express.

audio.lecture: Walters 5784 Edited/Ch 37/037.1 Shaar HaYichud ch 37.1 enhanced.mp3

blocks.text: Torah is compared to Yaakov, Zeir Anpin, and it has two aspects. Its inner part comes from seeing the chachma in a Jewish *neshama*, the G-dliness in things and the potential in them; its real essence is to unlock that potential and nurture it. From that inner part one must understand the situation and see how to deal with it. Then comes the outer voice, the *psak* that says to do this or not to do that. That is the revealed part of Torah.

audio.lecture: Walters 5784 Edited/Ch 37/037.1 Shaar HaYichud ch 37.1 enhanced.mp3

blocks.text: The verse in *Tehillim*, *yom leyom yabi'a omer*, teaches that every day we learn something new. The letters *alef*, *mem*, *resh* of *omer* stand for *esh*, *mayim* and *ruach*: fire, water and wind, which correspond to three middos, *chesed*, *gevura* and *tiferes*. Every emotion is a mixture of them: do we like it, are we afraid of it?

audio.lecture: Walters 5784 Edited/Ch 37/037.1 Shaar HaYichud ch 37.1 enhanced.mp3

blocks.text: Just as the physical voice is made of air from the lungs, with a balance between the dry and the moist, which is the fire and the water in it, so the spiritual breath of the heart is made of fire, water and wind. A person's emotional state is heard in the voice: whether he is happy or sad, that drives what he expresses and what moves him to speak.

audio.lecture: Walters 5784 Edited/Ch 37/037.1 Shaar HaYichud ch 37.1 enhanced.mp3

blocks.text: The breath of the heart is the feeling of *chesed* and *gevura*. *Chesed* is wanting to go towards something and to have more of it; *gevura* is wanting to hold back and move away. A person has to weigh the two and put them together, and the balance between them is the *ruach*, the middle.

sections.summary: Each breath of the heart is an expansion for joy (chesed), a contraction for sadness (gevura), or a balance between them (tiferes). Fire dries the voice, water makes it crisp, and the balanced voice holds tension in hope.

blocks.text: The spiritual breath of the heart contracts and expands. A sad or depressed person withdraws and does not want to speak; a happy one wants to talk and express himself. Both feelings are in the spiritual breath of the heart.

audio.lecture: Walters 5784 Edited/Ch 37/037.1 Shaar HaYichud ch 37.1 enhanced.mp3

blocks.text: Why is it called the *hevel* of the heart if it comes from the lungs? There is a simple answer and a deeper one. The simple answer is that the Torah names and classifies things differently than modern medicine or modern speech. As he understands it from his research, the Torah looks at whole body systems: it calls the whole cardiovascular system the heart, and the air in the lungs part of the heart's system.

audio.lecture: Walters 5784 Edited/Ch 37/037.1 Shaar HaYichud ch 37.1 enhanced.mp3

blocks.text: The deeper answer, in Kabbalah, is that an idea starts in the mind. From the mind it goes into the heart as a speech that tells the heart how to feel, and that inner voice gives rise to a spiritual breath that creates our emotional state. That is not physical breath; it is closer to hormones and electrochemical impulses that set how fast the heart beats. That breath is then composed into the physical breath in the lungs, the outer part of the heart, which comes out in the physical voice. So there are two parts.

audio.lecture: Walters 5784 Edited/Ch 37/037.1 Shaar HaYichud ch 37.1 enhanced.mp3

blocks.text: The *hevel* of the heart is that spiritual breath, the emotional state. *Ruach* can also mean a spirit, as in high or low spirits, so this emotional state is a spirit.

blocks.text: A good voice, and a good song, has a balance: not only happy and not only sad, but both together. Good mental and emotional health is also about this balance. *Chassidus* wants us to feel a tension: we have all this potential and will never quite live up to it, so there is always more to do. Feeling hopeful and able to overcome, while knowing there is challenge, is that balance.

sections.title: Life is breathing in and out: the heart's expansion and contraction
sections.summary: The rhythm of breath and heartbeat is the rhythm of life. The air of life is both oxygen and consciousness, and the pattern of going out and coming back, rotzo and shov, runs through the body, the heart and divine service.

blocks.title: Chabad niggunim
blocks.text: I think Chabad *niggunim* tend to have that balance. Many are in a minor key, which is sad, yet many are happy anyway, with a balance of complexity.

audio.lecture: Walters 5784 Edited/Ch 37/037.1 Shaar HaYichud ch 37.1 enhanced.mp3

blocks.text: *Ruach chayim* has a physical and a spiritual counterpart. Physically it is the air that oxygenates the blood and gives the ability to live and be conscious. If a limb falls asleep and loses its feeling, or on a flight when the cabin loses pressure and you must first put on your own mask, the lack of oxygen is what does it: about thirty seconds without enough oxygen is enough to lose consciousness.

audio.lecture: Walters 5784 Edited/Ch 37/037.1 Shaar HaYichud ch 37.1 enhanced.mp3

blocks.text: *Ruach chayim* also has a spiritual counterpart: the consciousness that comes from the mind, which goes into the right side of the heart and then the left, from *chachma*. In *Kabbalah*, *ruach* is the more internal part of the voice and *hevel* the more external; the pattern is *rotzo v'shov*.

audio.lecture: Walters 5784 Edited/Ch 37/037.1 Shaar HaYichud ch 37.1 enhanced.mp3

blocks.text: The heart and lungs work the same way: contraction and expansion. Life is this constant balance: breathing in expands the lungs to let in air, breathing out contracts them. The heart opens to take in blood and contracts to push it out.

audio.lecture: Walters 5784 Edited/Ch 37/037.1 Shaar HaYichud ch 37.1 enhanced.mp3

blocks.text: Life is a back and forth: someone who thinks only "I am happy and successful" never does anything, and so does someone who thinks only "I am a failure." Life means a goal not yet reached, then reached, then a new goal that makes what you have feel not good enough.

audio.lecture: Walters 5784 Edited/Ch 37/037.1 Shaar HaYichud ch 37.1 enhanced.mp3

blocks.text: He ties this to the opening chapters, five and six: in any *hisbonenus* there must be a sense on the one hand of joy in what one can understand, and on the other of humility and awe before the G-dly *ein* that one cannot grasp. A balance between those two is always needed.

The metaphor: once a king issues a decree it must be carried out, but a wish he has not yet spoken is not a decree and need not happen. Once he says it, as in the *Megillah*, a stamped decree cannot be retracted. G-d's speech is what actually creates the world, from nothing; the *mashal* and *nimshal* come later.

blocks.text: This is the *chesed*, *gevura* and *tiferes* of the breath of the heart of *Zeir Anpin*, which unites with speech. Understanding it gives three basic levels.

audio.lecture: Walters 5784 Edited/Ch 37/037.2 Shaar HaYichud ch 37.2 enhanced.mp3

blocks.title: The feeling you can take back
blocks.text: The first level is in us, ordinary psychology: we have emotions, and they can be heard in the voice, affecting whether we feel like speaking. Once a person says something, he cannot take it back: a hurtful word cannot be undone, and neither can a kind one. But as long as it is only in the feelings, you can rethink it and change your perspective. That is the metaphor in us.

audio.lecture: Walters 5784 Edited/Ch 37/037.2 Shaar HaYichud ch 37.2 enhanced.mp3

blocks.text: The second level is *Torah* and *avoda*. In the revealed part of Torah, the *halacha*, the middos come into speech. A *rav* weighs many factors, but once the sages decide a *halacha*, that is it, and it cannot be changed. When *Beis Shammai* and *Beis Hillel* debated, there was a point where both ways were open. But once they voted and the *Sanhedrin* decided, that became *halacha*, even though both opinions are the words of the living G-d. The Torah has room for many opinions, but once something is decided it is *halacha*.

audio.lecture: Walters 5784 Edited/Ch 37/037.2 Shaar HaYichud ch 37.2 enhanced.mp3

blocks.text: The third level is the world, created by G-d's speech and words, so everything physical around us is G-d's speech. In *Tanya*, in *Shaar HaYichud VeHaEmuna*, the middos are: *chesed* creates something from nothing; *gevura* is the *tzimtzum* that hides G-dliness so that we feel independent; and *tiferes* balances the two, so that through revelations, miracles, the Torah and the *tzaddikim* we can appreciate G-dliness despite the *tzimtzum*.

audio.lecture: Walters 5784 Edited/Ch 37/037.2 Shaar HaYichud ch 37.2 enhanced.mp3

blocks.text: This relates to *midda k'neged midda* and *hashgacha prat*: G-d creates the world with certain middos, but He gives us an ability to change, and when we change we get different things. Some things are just created: once *Hashem* says a thing will be, that is how it is, like the laws of nature, and angels are created from G-d's speech and cannot change. But some things are in the middos, in the heart, and G-d looks at what we do and based on it He may reconsider. That is the basis even of science and technology: if we learn and change how we interact with the world, we get different results, and morally too.

audio.lecture: Walters 5784 Edited/Ch 37/037.2 Shaar HaYichud ch 37.2 enhanced.mp3

blocks.text: Now the other side: the *pnimiyus* of *Yisrael* and *Leah*, the hidden world, *alma d'isachsya*. Touched on earlier with the circles and the straight line, this is central in *Kabbalah*, as the *Ramak* says: we want to live in both the spiritual and physical worlds. The world has two parts: the external, created by G-d's speech and middos, and the internal, created by His *mochin*. Souls come from G-d's thought, angels from His speech. Torah is the idea of the *mochin*, and the world is the idea of the middos.

audio.lecture: Walters 5784 Edited/Ch 37/037.2 Shaar HaYichud ch 37.2 enhanced.mp3

blocks.title: Ink on paper
blocks.text: Look at a book: objectively it is ink on paper, and it need not mean anything. We give meaning to those symbols, and a whole other world is hidden in the book, one that exists inside the mind of the reader. In a similar way G-d puts a *neshama* inside us, with an intuition and a nature that want to be curious, to learn, to know what is true, good and beautiful, and a conscience that wants to do what is right. That is our internal world, parallel to the external physical world. It is the realm of Torah, and within Torah it is the realm of *pnimiyus haTorah*.

blocks.text: He says he has been reading a book on this, and that certain internal thoughts create certain feelings. If a person reads a situation as a violation of his rights, he becomes angry; if he reads it as a loss of something or of his self-worth, he becomes sad; if he reads it as how others will view him and whether he lives up to his values, he feels embarrassment or shame. These are different internal monologues, ways of narrating what happened, and the interpretation is what creates the middos. The feeling comes from inside you, projected onto the event. Between the event and the feeling there is a *sechel*, an interpretation we read into it. Change that and you change how you feel: this is the idea of *mocha shelit al haLev*, the mind ruling the heart. He notes that people call this framing.

audio.lecture: Walters 5784 Edited/Ch 37/037.2 Shaar HaYichud ch 37.2 enhanced.mp3

blocks.text: There is an objective event, such as an experiment with a result, or walking into a wall and being stopped, which is a message, and maybe a little *gevura* in it. Then we build a model and a narrative to interpret the data. That model is in our mind, and it is only partly connected to the world. It can help us predict, and sometimes it is a parallel reality that does not predict anything. The *Rambam*, in the *Moreh Nevuchim*, treats such things as philosophical rather than scientific. Anything that cannot be tested in the world is like that, including the past, which cannot be tested, so one can make a story of it.

audio.lecture: Walters 5784 Edited/Ch 37/037.2 Shaar HaYichud ch 37.2 enhanced.mp3

blocks.text: Today in science there is a kind of religion around this: they tell stories of the distant past, of our ancestors as cavemen, and have no idea whether these are true. They are narratives with no real scientific or predictive value, and people like having the sense of meaning and purpose they put on top. So one must separate the objective thing from the story put over it.

audio.lecture: Walters 5784 Edited/Ch 37/037.2 Shaar HaYichud ch 37.2 enhanced.mp3

sensitivity.reason: Calls scientists' accounts of the past a religion and says they have no idea whether they are true. A criticism of a profession, which a public reader may take as contempt for scientists.
sensitivity.publishable: Today in science there is a lot of this: they tell stories of the distant past, of our ancestors as cavemen. They are narratives with no real scientific or predictive value, and people like having the sense of meaning and purpose they put on top. So one must separate the objective thing from the story put over it.

blocks.text: The same is true of our emotions. What happened is objective, but we lay a whole narrative over it, much of which we cannot know to be true or prove. That can be very powerful on the other hand, because if we change how we think, we change how we feel and how we act.

audio.lecture: Walters 5784 Edited/Ch 37/037.2 Shaar HaYichud ch 37.2 enhanced.mp3

blocks.text: In Torah there is the revealed part, *halacha*, and the inner part, *aggada*, with its *midrashim* and *remazim*. Where do they come from? The *Zohar* says that one must have an idea that is already true, see its inner truth, and then put that interpretation into words as a *drush*. A *drush* is more flexible than a *halacha*, where the *psak* has to be a certain way. An *aggada* that inspires people to do good and more good comes from a true place, so it is a valid way to look at things.

audio.lecture: Walters 5784 Edited/Ch 37/037.2 Shaar HaYichud ch 37.2 enhanced.mp3

blocks.text: A story can be very powerful. There is a letter of the Rebbe about levels within ourselves: a part five years old, one ten, one thirteen, one seventy. We need different stories to motivate those parts, and that is okay.

audio.lecture: Walters 5784 Edited/Ch 37/037.2 Shaar HaYichud ch 37.2 enhanced.mp3

blocks.text: Sometimes, as the Rebbe says there, you tell yourself the food grew from manure, so do not be so excited: it all comes from filth. blocks.title: The Baal Shem Tov and the child
blocks.text: A couple who had waited years for a child lost him at two or three. They went to the *Baal Shem Tov*, who told them that the child's soul was the *gilgul* of a Jew raised by a non-Jewish noble family, who learned he was Jewish only at the end of his life. He wanted to convert, and I think in the end he did and went up to *Gan Eden*, but he had never nursed from a Jewish mother. So he came back in a new *gilgul* to nurse from a Jewish mother, and then he could go to *olam haba*. The story did not change the tragedy, but it gave them a deep sense of meaning and purpose.

audio.lecture: Walters 5784 Edited/Ch 37/037.2 Shaar HaYichud ch 37.2 enhanced.mp3

blocks.text: That is the power of a sense of meaning and purpose. The same is true of *kavana* in the *mitzvos*: it does not necessarily change what you physically do, but it can give a lot of inspiration and meaning to it.

audio.lecture: Walters 5784 Edited/Ch 37/037.2 Shaar HaYichud ch 37.2 enhanced.mp3

blocks.text: Within this inner voice is a mix of fire, water and wind, the middos of *chesed*, *gevura* and *tiferes*, in the inner part of the heart. It is looking into yourself: who am I, what do I want to express? An essential desire for kindness, for independence, for what is essential to me.

audio.lecture: Walters 5784 Edited/Ch 37/037.2 Shaar HaYichud ch 37.2 enhanced.mp3

blocks.text: These middos carry the light of the *mochin*, the inner voice of *binah*. Emotions are not only natural wiring. blocks.text: The external reality is science and systems, while the *middos* respond *midda k'neged midda* to how we act. The internal reality we can change is a sense of who we are and our purpose. G-d creates that whole separate side of reality, inside us, so in that sense we help create the world by how we look at it. As far as we know, all the meaning of the universe is in our tiny speck, the only place we know of with people with a sense of meaning and purpose; in that sense we are like the center of the universe.

audio.lecture: Walters 5784 Edited/Ch 37/037.2 Shaar HaYichud ch 37.2 enhanced.mp3

blocks.text: Understanding these two parallel layers, the external and the internal, and how they relate, is a big thing in understanding Torah, ourselves and reality. Sometimes a sense of meaning or a narrative makes us more or less effective and affects the external. Sometimes the two stay parallel, and a person does what he does while thinking about it differently. And sometimes an event outside makes us rethink everything. The two can relate in many ways.
